GTA VI Console Graphics Settings Revealed: Higher Framerate Theoretically Possible on PS5 Pro

Since the launch of GTA VI, gamers, modders, and hackers alike have been hacking away at the game's files to see what they can break, whether that be in order to unofficially port the game to PC, find workarounds to Rockstar's limitations, or just for interest's sake. This time, it seems as though it's the latter. A dataminer who goes by Tex2 on X and the GTA forums has discovered the graphics options for the various console versions of GTA VI, revealing what options have been enabled on various gaming consoles and perhaps even giving us an idea of what to expect from the eventual PC port of GTA VI.
Interestingly, the base PlayStation 5 and the Xbox Series X both run identical graphics presets, while the PS5 Pro has additional ray tracing options enabled, and the Xbox Series S has the least demanding settings preset. The original post on X has seemingly been removed without explanation, but the full list of settings is still available thanks to reporting by MP1st and Notebookcheck. Interestingly, the GTA VI graphics settings are mostly set to high on the PS5 Pro, with a few medium settings scattered throughout. The ray tracing settings, which are notoriously demanding on hardware, stand out as also being set to high on Sony's high-end console. Even the base PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X have most settings set to high or medium, with ray tracing disabled. It's been previously shown that disabling the 30 FPS limit on the Xbox Series X will result in GTA VI running as high as 50-60 FPS in some scenarios, but mostly hovering around 45 FPS, and these settings suggest that there is room for graphical quality to be reduced in order to reach a higher framerate at the cost of some realism, especially on the PS5 Pro, which has a number of graphical settings set to Ultra. This is also good news for PC gamers, since the PS5 Pro has internals more or less equivalent to something between the AMD Radeon RX 6800 and 7800 with some extra RDNA 4 ray tracing tech in the mix. This means that, provided Rockstar delivers a solid port of GTA VI on PC, most PCs running a GPU like an NVIDIA RTX 4070 or faster should be able to match the image quality and performance of the PS5 Pro in GTA VI. A modern Ryzen 7 or Intel Core Ultra 7 desktop chip should also have more than enough CPU power to handle the simulation and other CPU-bound tasks in GTA VI.

Modern GPUs are no longer used exclusively for gaming and 3D rendering. They also support an expanding range of local AI workloads, including image and video processing. For PC enthusiasts with large collections of older recordings, compressed clips, or low-resolution footage, AI video enhancement offers another practical use for desktop computing power.
Browser-based solutions such as NVIDIA RTX Video Super Resolution can improve the appearance of supported streaming content during playback. However, users who want to enhance and export their own video files need a different kind of workflow—one that can address noise, blur, compression artifacts, and resolution limitations in the source footage.
One example is Aiarty Video Enhancer, a desktop AI application for Windows and macOS that uses dedicated models to improve existing video footage. It offers tools for reducing noise, sharpening blurry or pixelated footage, and increasing resolution. The software supports NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, as well as CPU processing. Video files are processed locally without cloud uploads or processing credits, and users can enhance multiple clips in batches with output resolutions up to 4K.

AI Video Upscaling: Bring Low-Resolution Footage Up to 4K
A low-resolution gameplay recording, for example, may look soft or pixelated when viewed on a larger monitor or reused in a video project. The same issue can affect footage captured with older devices, cropped video clips, screen recordings, and AI-generated videos that lack sufficient resolution for their intended use.
Aiarty Video Enhancer supports 2x, 4x, and custom scaling, with output resolutions up to 4K. Its AI models analyze visual patterns to estimate missing details, sharpen edges, and improve textures during enlargement, helping turn low-resolution footage into clearer HD or 4K videos.
AI Video Deblurring: Sharpen Blurry and Pixelated Footage
Anime clips, downloaded videos, and gameplay captures can lose visual clarity due to low resolution, compression, or repeated resizing. This may result in blocky artifacts, jagged edges, and a general loss of fine details, particularly when viewed on a larger screen. Simply increasing sharpness can make compression artifacts more noticeable rather than restore useful details.
Instead of simply applying a sharpening filter, Aiarty Video Enhancer uses AI processing to sharpen edges, enhance visible details, and reduce distracting pixelation. This helps give footage that has lost clarity a cleaner, more defined look, making fine textures and visual elements easier to distinguish. AI Video Denoising: Remove Noise While Preserving Details
Nighttime recordings, indoor videos, and footage shot at high ISO settings often contain visible grain or colored noise. These imperfections can become more noticeable when editing clips or watching them on a larger display.
The superVideo vHQ model in Aiarty Video Enhancer is designed specifically for noisy and low-light footage. It helps reduce visible noise while preserving important image details, making grainy recordings cleaner without unnecessarily smoothing out textures. Adjust Colors and Convert SDR to HDR for More Vivid Video
Older recordings and footage captured under challenging lighting conditions may look dull, washed out, or lack contrast. Color and lighting adjustments can help improve their overall appearance, making details and colors more visible.
Aiarty Video Enhancer provides controls for adjusting exposure, contrast, saturation, and other color settings, giving users more flexibility to fine-tune the overall look of their footage. It also supports SDR-to-HDR conversion with 10-bit output, allowing users to convert SDR videos into HDR output for compatible displays. AI Frame Interpolation: Create Smoother Motion
Gameplay recordings captured at 30 FPS can look less fluid when played on high-refresh-rate monitors. The same applies to action footage and other videos with fast-moving subjects. Frame interpolation can help by generating additional frames between the original ones.
Aiarty Video Enhancer supports AI frame interpolation with output options of 60, 90, and 120 FPS, allowing users to increase the frame rate of existing clips for smoother playback or video projects. AI models analyze motion between frames to generate intermediate images, helping create more fluid transitions between movements.
Harnessing Desktop Compute with Local AI Video Enhancement
When tackling heavy video enhancement tasks—such as upscaling a 25-minute standard-definition archive to crisp 4K—cloud-based solutions quickly run into bottlenecks. Subscription fees pile up, file size limits constrain workflows, and privacy concerns arise when uploading personal or proprietary footage to external servers.
Running optimization models locally on your own GPU, Aiarty changes the equation entirely:

  • GPU Acceleration & Optimized AI Models: Aiarty supports NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple Silicon GPUs, as well as CPU processing. Its optimized AI models are designed to improve inference efficiency while maintaining visual quality. A dedicated Turbo Mode can further speed up processing with a subtle trade-off in output quality.
  • Local Processing & Privacy: Video files are processed directly on your computer without uploading them to cloud servers or relying on cloud processing credits. This gives users more control over personal recordings and other video files.
  • Batch Processing: Multiple video files can be added to the enhancement workflow and processed in batches, making it easier to work through collections of recordings without handling each clip individually.
Final Thoughts
We have reached a point where desktop hardware capacity is no longer the primary bottleneck in video restoration- having software optimized to saturate those hardware pipelines is what makes the difference. From polishing screen captures and enhancing digital camera footage to restoring legacy video archives, deep-learning models are making local video processing more practical than ever.

NVIDIA Cuts RTX 50-Series Supply as RTX 60-Series Faces Possible Delay, Per Reports

NVIDIA celebrated Jensen Huang's return this week, but that doesn't mean the GPU shortage is over. In fact, reports from the Chinese distribution forum Board Channels claim that NVIDIA is planning to cut RTX 50-series supply even further. Apparently, NVIDIA's board partners will get 20-30% fewer gaming GPUs over the next three months, which covers the fourth quarter running from November 2026 through January 2027. The report, spotted by Videocardz, claims that NVIDIA has already notified its add-in-card (AIC) partners of the cut. We know that GPU supply to China has been extremely tight from NVIDIA's side, and this is expected to make the situation even worse for consumers. The post focuses only on China, but we may see NVIDIA implement the same policy in other regions, as it has before.
NVIDIA's tight supply is directly linked to AI demand, as corroborated by a report from Taiwan's Commercial Times. Taiwanese ODMs told the paper that new B300 orders take 26 to 40 weeks to deliver, while the delivery window for GB300 is around 14 to 26 weeks. Other products such as the RTX Pro accelerator cards and DGX Station have even stretched past that. To cope with that, NVIDIA is reportedly cutting back on GeForce RTX 50-series supply, as indicated by the Board Channels report. Industry sources expect that the wafers which are freed as a result of these cuts will go towards data center chips in order to meet demand. There's also the issue of memory, and we have covered plenty of reports about memory makers shifting their production pipelines towards AI customers. Then, there's the RTX 60-series consumer graphics cards, which are seemingly still quite a long time away. The Commercial Times also claims that the RTX 60-series could slip further due to the current situation. Those Rubin-based consumer graphics cards were targeting mass production by the end of 2027, but it looks like that timeline will be pushed back. This also lines up with previous leaks that the RTX 60-series has been delayed to 2028. No new 60-series cards means that board partners will have to rely on 50-series for longer, and even that is facing severe shortages.
We saw GPU makers steering distributors towards RTX 30-series cards earlier this month as RTX 50 stock dried up, while the Blackwell cards have seen multiple price hikes over the past few months. NVIDIA also reportedly trimmed AIC supply by 15-20% back in January, and now we have another reduction on our hands. With this, buyers should expect even fewer RTX 50-series cards, as well as higher prices, heading into the new year.

articles.title: Supermicro SYS-E103-14P-H Review: A Fanless Panther Lake Edge Appliance
articles.summary: The Supermicro SYS-E103-14P-H is an interesting little fanless appliance that pairs Intel's new Panther Lake Core Ultra X7 368H processor with a dense industrial I/O layout The post Supermicro SYS-E103-14P-H Review: A Fanless Panther Lake Edge Appliance appeared first on ServeTheHome .
articles.content_html:
The Supermicro SYS-E103-14P-H is an interesting little fanless appliance that pairs Intel’s new Panther Lake Core Ultra X7 368H processor with a dense industrial I/O layout. It packs a heterogeneous 16-core CPU, replaceable SODIMM memory and M.2 storage into a finned chassis that Supermicro rates for fanless operation in edge deployments.

Supermicro SYS-E103-14P-H Key Specs (As Reviewed)
Processor Intel Core Ultra X7 368H, 4P + 8E + 4 LPE (5.0GHz)
Operating System Ubuntu Linux 26.04 LTS
Memory 32GB DDR5-5600 (2x16GB SODIMM)
Storage256GB SSD (M.2 2280/2242, PCIe Gen5 x4)

1x M.2 2280 PCIe Gen4 x2 (Empty)
GPU Intel Arc B390 (Xe3, 12 Xe cores)
PSU 150W External Adapter
Form Factor SFF Industrial PC
Dimensions 185 x 83 x 140 mm (7.28 x 3.27 x 5.5in)
Weight 1.47kg (3.25 lbs)
Networking2x 2.5GbE (Intel I226-IT)

1x 1GbE (Intel I219-LM)
Wireless Empty (M.2 2230 E-Key Slot Available)
Color Black
PortsFront:

2x 10Gbps USB-A, 4x 480Mbps USB-A, 2x HDMI 2.1, 2x 2.5GbE (RJ45), 1x 1GbE (RJ45), 2x COM (RS232), 1x GPIO (DB9)

Let us get to it.

Supermicro SYS-E103-14P-H External Overview

Here is the front panel of the E103-14P-H, showing a dense array of industrial I/O. You can see three RJ45 Ethernet jacks labeled LAN1 through LAN3, alongside four white USB 2.0 Type-A ports and two red USB 3.2 Gen2 connectors.

The front panel of the E103-14P-H carries most of the connectivity. This industrial gateway-style layout puts nearly everything you need to cable on one face. The chassis itself measures 185 x 83 x 140mm (7.28″ x 3.27″ x 5.5″) per Supermicro’s datasheet, which makes it a compact box that can sit on a DIN rail or behind an edge display.

The front face is a dense black panel with the two DB9 COM ports on the bottom row. A blue GPIO connector sits at the left edge of this same panel, while RJ45, USB, HDMI, and DC connectors fill out the rest of the layout.

Let us get into some of these a bit closer, starting with power.

The front panel places the power button on the right side adjacent to two indicator lamps. A close-up of the status LEDs reveals two distinct indicators: an amber light marked with a cylinder icon for storage activity, and a green light marked with a bulb icon for system power. These sit just above the main power button on the front bezel.

The network configuration deserves a closer look because it is not uniform. The system has two Intel I226-IT controllers driving the 2.5GbE ports, plus one Intel I219-LM controller for the single 1GbE port. That third port supports Intel vPro management so while there is no IPMI, you get vPro. We captured all three interfaces in Linux: eno1 and eno2 are the I226-IT parts on PCIe root ports, while eno3 is the I219-LM integrated into the PCH.

Two white USB Type-A connectors sit above the LAN ports. These are USB 2.0 interfaces, which Supermicro specifies for low-speed peripherals and industrial accessories that do not require higher bandwidth.

The USB 2.0 ports are useful for low-speed peripherals like dongles and serial adapters without wasting the faster USB 3.2 Gen2 ports on the red connectors. For an edge gateway, that is a sensible split because many industrial accessories do not need more than USB 2.0 bandwidth.

Next to the final Ethernet jack, two red Type-A ports are stacked vertically with SuperSpeed USB markings. These provide USB 3.2 Gen2 connectivity for faster external storage or other high-bandwidth devices.

Moving across the front panel, two HDMI 2.1 ports provide display output from the integrated Intel Arc B390 GPU. The processor supports up to four displays per Intel’s specifications, and Supermicro exposes two of them on this chassis. Next to those are two male DB9 connectors labeled as COM ports supporting RS-232/422/485.

Below the USB and video outputs, a male DB9 connector labeled COM1 is visible. This port supports RS-232/422/485 serial communication, providing legacy industrial interface options alongside modern networking.

This close-up shows the second serial connector, labeled COM2. It is a male DB9 port with nine pins and two threaded standoffs for securing cables.

The blue female DB9 port on this system is an 8-bit GPIO/SMBus interface.

The locking DC input sits at the right end of the front panel. Supermicro rates this system for 12V to 36V wide-range DC input, which is a useful feature for industrial sites with existing DC power distribution rather than standard AC outlets. A locking connector is great, since you do not want someone to pull the power out if this is running automation for systems on an assembly line or running an important digital signage kiosk (as examples.)

The enclosure itself does most of the thermal work here since there are no fans. The top and bottom surfaces carry pronounced cooling fins that increase surface area for passive heat dissipation. This is a common approach in fanless industrial systems, where the chassis metal becomes the heatsink.

The side panel features three antenna knockouts marked ANT. These openings allow wireless module connectors to pass through when an M.2 radio card is installed.

The rear of the unit is comparatively sparse because most I/O moved to the front. Antenna knockouts on the rear and sides support wireless modules, which can be used with the M.2 E-key slot inside that can host a Wi-Fi or other radio card.

There are plenty of knockouts for putting antennas around this chassis.

You can use this box and then have antennas come out of the different sides depending on how you mount it, which we can see being handy in tighter installations.

The underside has much shallower heatsink fins.

Here is the mounting bracket.

With that, let us open the enclosure to examine the mainboard layout and internal components.

Wednesday, November 25th 2026

SK hynix to Start 3D DRAM Production in 2031

SK hynix is planning to begin mass production of next-generation 3D DRAM by 2031, confirmed Choi Kang-sik, a Distinguished Engineer at SK hynix, during the AI Semiconductor Forum at Seoul National University in Gwanak-gu. According to the presentation, SK hynix's roadmap indicates that 3D DRAM production could start in 4 to 5 years, which would place the timeline at the latest in 2031. SK hynix estimates that 3D DRAM would require approximately 75 memory layers to match the memory density of today's leading-edge 1c DRAM, which utilizes a 10 nm class design. Considering other factors, the company aims to develop a 100-layer design as a first-generation product to ensure it represents a significant advancement over the planar DRAM it has been manufacturing for years.
Current equipment can reportedly handle 100 layers of 3D DRAM, but achieving 200 to 300-layer DRAM would require multi-deck stacking and specialized hybrid bonding techniques, adapted from 3D NAND flash, to reach higher densities. SK hynix is expected to adopt this technology from the Chinese company YMTC and license its Xtacking technology. Xtacking hybrid bonding creates a permanent bond between two silicon chips using embedded metal bumps that are fused together to form a single chip. Multiple dies or entire silicon wafers can be connected by stacking the back ends of two chips together. Both SK hynix and Samsung see this as a potential method to advance their 3D NAND production. As SK hynix plans to apply this 3D NAND flash technology to 3D DRAM, we are only a few years away from seeing it in action. SK hynix currently manufactures a type of 3D memory in the form of HBM, but it is essentially regular DRAM stacked in multiple layers. To achieve true 3D DRAM, SK hynix will need to change the underlying architecture and completely overhaul its DRAM manufacturing process. This shift is likely to occur once YMTC's Xtacking technology enters production.

articles.summary: Almost two weeks ago, we reported on Apex Neural Rendering (ANR), an ambitious open-source alternative to NVIDIA DLSS promising superior image quality, faster frame generation processing, and considerably lower VRAM consumption across a wide range of GPUs. articles.content_html:
Almost two weeks ago, we reported on Apex Neural Rendering (ANR), an ambitious open-source alternative to NVIDIA DLSS promising superior image quality, faster frame generation processing, and considerably lower VRAM consumption across a wide range of GPUs.

We subsequently put the technology through its paces in three PC games, uncovering promising results alongside several shortcomings. Now, Digital Foundry has conducted its own independent analysis, with similarly encouraging, albeit mixed, findings.

Apex Neural Rendering Trades Blows With NVIDIA DLSS, But Still Needs More Polish

Digital Foundry tested ANR on a PC featuring an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti, and 32 GB of DDR5-6000 memory.

In Marvel's Spider-Man Remastered at 4K with DLAA and 2X Frame Generation, ANR achieved 130.5 FPS compared to NVIDIA DLSS FG's 124.9 FPS, alongside broadly comparable frame pacing and PC latency.

However, the tables turned at higher frame generation multipliers. NVIDIA DLSS MFG was approximately 10% faster in Cyberpunk 2077 at 3X with path tracing enabled, while Crimson Desert at 4X saw ANR trail NVIDIA's solution by just 3.6%, with virtually identical PC latency.

Image quality comparisons revealed some familiar shortcomings, including increased ghosting, difficulties handling UI elements, and less reliable detection of camera cuts. Nevertheless, ANR occasionally produced less noticeable interpolation artifacts than DLSS, particularly in The Last of Us Part II.

These findings largely echo our own testing: ANR is remarkably competitive for beta software developed by a single individual, but NVIDIA DLSS remains the more polished solution overall.

Apex Neural Rendering Brings Multi Frame Generation To Older AMD And Intel GPUs

Perhaps more compelling is ANR's ability to run through conventional compute shaders rather than relying on dedicated machine learning acceleration.

Digital Foundry tested ANR 3X Multi Frame Generation in Cyberpunk 2077 at 1440p on Intel's Arc B580 and AMD's Radeon RX 6700, achieving 186 FPS and 149 FPS, respectively.

However, average PC latency reached 67 ms and 82 ms, respectively, with the Radeon GPU also exhibiting uneven frame pacing.

While further optimization is clearly necessary, ANR's potential to extend advanced Multi Frame Generation capabilities to older graphics cards remains one of its strongest selling points.

Apex Compute's New Tool Could Revolutionize Image Quality Comparisons

Arguably the most exciting revelation from Digital Foundry's analysis is Apex Compute's new frame-accurate recording and comparison tool.

Rather than recording conventional gameplay footage, the tool captures the raw inputs supplied to frame generation and upscaling algorithms, allowing different implementations to process identical frames offline.

This eliminates discrepancies in lighting, particle effects, character movements, and other variables that traditionally complicate image quality comparisons. It also allows reviewers to isolate artificially generated frames for closer inspection.

The biggest caveat? Digital Foundry's comparison footage required approximately 1 TB of raw captured data, making fast, high-capacity SSDs particularly desirable.

Nevertheless, this could fundamentally change how reviewers evaluate technologies such as NVIDIA DLSS, AMD FSR, Intel XeSS, and ANR going forward.

With Apex Compute's Super Resolution and Ray Reconstruction technologies still in development, we're certainly looking forward to seeing what this newcomer has in store for PC gamers.

According to Nikkei Asia, South Korea's largest chipmakers are currently looking to license technology from China's YMTC. Specifically, SK hynix and Samsung are exploring ways to integrate YMTC's highly successful Xtacking silicon 3D NAND design. In the fourth iteration of Xtacking, YMTC can separate memory cell wafers from peripheral logic circuits and combine them using hybrid bonding wafer-to-wafer stacking. Multiple dies or entire silicon wafers can be connected by stacking the back ends of two chips together, and SK hynix and Samsung see this as a potential way to advance their 3D NAND production.

Since 2019, YMTC has been manufacturing using Xtacking technology, now on version 4.0. Samsung told Nikkei Asia that this bonding technology offers numerous advantages over the current approach to building many-layer NAND flash. SK hynix and Samsung are building NAND with hundreds of layers but are hitting single-wafer limitations. YMTC's technology has been refined and production-tested, making it easier for Samsung and SK hynix to switch to it. Additionally, YMTC has filed more than 4,000 patents related to 3D memory production, packaging, and more since 2018. For Samsung and SK hynix, it is much easier to license the technology from YMTC to avoid legal disputes instead of developing their own path.

articles.content_html:
Following the recent controversy surrounding AMD and NVIDIA's graphics drivers excessively writing data to SSDs, it appears that even seemingly harmless browser extensions could be contributing to premature storage wear. One Windows 11 user has traced an alarming amount of background write activity to the official Adobe Acrobat Google Chrome extension, which boasts over 350 million users worldwide.

Adobe Acrobat's Chrome Extension Reportedly Keeps Generating Excessive Write Activity Even When The Browser Is Closed

In a recent Reddit post, user xenius_ykk detailed how they investigated unusually high storage activity on their largely idle Windows 11 PC. Using PowerShell, the user discovered that Chrome had accumulated over 300GB of write I/O activity in approximately three days, despite its local cache occupying just 3.5GB.

The investigation pointed to an Adobe-associated service worker, which appeared to be repeatedly populating and replacing approximately 1GB of cached data. The activity reportedly persisted overnight, even with Chrome's windows closed.

For those unfamiliar, service workers allow browsers to perform various background tasks independently of an active webpage, including caching resources and handling notifications.

After uninstalling the Adobe Acrobat extension, unregistering the associated service worker, clearing its site data, and restarting Chrome, the user reported that idle write activity decreased from approximately 730MB to 135MB over a five-minute interval, a reduction of more than 81%.

It should be noted, however, that Windows' WriteTransferCount metric also encompasses non-storage I/O, including network transfers. As such, the reported 300GB figure should not be interpreted as a definitive measurement of physical SSD writes.

This Isn't The First Time Adobe's Popular Chrome Extension Has Been Associated With Storage-Related Issues

Interestingly, a separate report published on Adobe's official community forums in May 2026 detailed how the same extension was allegedly filling up storage drives across multiple enterprise PCs by repeatedly generating 4MB log files.

Removing the extension reportedly resolved the issue, with an Adobe employee subsequently requesting additional diagnostic information.

While it remains unclear whether the two incidents share the same underlying cause, the extension's enormous user base certainly makes these reports worth investigating. According to its official Chrome Web Store listing, Adobe Acrobat is among the browser's most widely installed extensions.

Here's How You Can Check Whether Background Applications Are Unnecessarily Wearing Out Your SSD

With both AMD and NVIDIA having recently experienced excessive SSD-writing issues, periodically monitoring your system's background storage activity might not be a bad idea.

Windows users can launch the built-in Resource Monitor by typing 

resmon
into the Start menu, navigating to the Disk tab, and sorting processes by their write activity. Meanwhile, Chrome users can inspect registered service workers through 
chrome://serviceworker-internals/
and review installed extensions through 
chrome://extensions/
.

Disabling Chrome's background application functionality under 

chrome://settings/system
may also help prevent unnecessary activity when the browser is closed.

Although modern SSDs feature considerable write endurance, unnecessary background writes can gradually consume that endurance without providing any tangible benefit to the user.

With storage prices under pressure, keeping an eye on what your software is doing behind the scenes could prove increasingly worthwhile.

The AI boom is already reshaping the consumer hardware market, but a growing race for high-end PCB could further apply more pressure on the GPUs and other PC components.

The AI Demand is Driving a New PCB Race That Could Impact Consumer Hardware, Reports Taiwan Printed Circuit Association

Last month's report by Nikkei Asia suggested that the hardware could become more expensive due to rising PCB costs. Many vendors complained that they weren't able to secure enough PCB supplies for hardware production, and now another report indicates growing competition to fulfill PCB demand for AI infrastructure.

According to TPCA (Taiwan Printed Circuit Association), the continued expansion of global AI infrastructure is driving demand for high-end printed circuit boards (PCBs), IC substrates, and high-speed interconnects. China, Japan, and South Korea are reportedly responding by strengthening their high-end manufacturing capabilities, supply chains, and advanced packaging technologies.

The report highlights how the AI demand is spreading beyond components like GPUs to ASICs, CPUs, and even networking chips, which has increased the demand for high-end substrates and server PCBs. In South Korea, AI chips are particularly driving the demand for larger and higher-layer-count ABF substrates, while DDR5, GDDR7, and SOCAMM memory applications are also increasing demand for BT substrates and module PCBs.

Based on the region of origin of corporate funds and including the output value of domestic and overseas production bases, China's PCB output value is estimated at US$47.71 billion in 2026, a year-on-year increase of 34.1%; Japan's is estimated at US$13.58 billion, a year-on-year increase of 12.9%; and South Korea's is estimated at US$11.07 billion, a year-on-year increase of 29.3%. China, Japan, and South Korea together account for over 60% of the global PCB market.

- TPCA

China is also shifting its focus towards more investment in AI computing and high-speed interconnects, with new capacity focused on high-layer-count PCBs and high-density interconnect boards used in AI servers. Japanese manufacturers, on the other hand, are benefiting from the growing demand for high-end substrates and server PCBs. However, the report notes that some key materials are already facing supply shortages and cost pressures.

All of this could have some significant consequences for the consumer hardware market. While the TPCA report doesn't say that the manufacturers are cutting PCB supplies for consumer-grade components, it's obvious that manufacturers will prioritize AI demand due to greater incentives. This could eventually make consumer hardware more expensive, particularly the GPUs, which need sophisticated PCBs, memory, power delivery components, and high-speed interconnects.

articles.summary: A number of new, unannounced Intel Core Ultra 4000-series chips have been detailed in a Nova Lake document, ahead of what is expected to be an official unveiling of the chips at a next-generation desktop chip event in Berlin, Germany, in February 2027.

7 new Intel Nova Lake-S Core Ultra 4000-series CPUs detailed in new leak — lineup includes 5.5GHz Ultra 9 4970K BFC, ahead of the expected February 2027 release

News

Oliver Haslam

The desktop chips range from 22 to 28 cores, featuring boost speeds up to 5.5 GHz, with manufacturers expected to show compatible motherboards at CES in January.

1

A newly leaked document purportedly details no less than seven new Nova Lake-S desktop processors based on C1 stepping qualification samples, including 28-core models, three months before Intel is expected to officially take the wraps off them. The new leak, from VideoCardz, includes an Intel warning that clock speeds and performance may change before the final products are ready to be shipped. But given the fact that this rarely happens when dealing with qualification samples, it's believed that the chips will likely be released just as they are outlined in the document, if the leak is accurate.

Of the seven chips that have been detailed, the top-of-the-line Core Ultra 9 4970K BFC will be the one of most interest. It will reportedly feature 28 cores comprising eight performance cores, 16 efficiency cores, and four low-power efficient cores. Its base efficiency core clock speed of 2.7 GHz is eclipsed by the 5.5 GHz boost speed its performance cores will reach, while 144 MB of L3 cache and a 125-watt power rating round out the main figures. According to the leak, it will be joined by a Core Ultra 9 4950K with the same core count and almost identical clock speeds, albeit with a much smaller 36 MB L3 cache. Beyond that, the report says the Core 9 4900 BFC will be locked at 65 watts, have 22 cores, and a 120 MB L3 cache.

If the leak holds up, the mid-range will be catered for by the Core Ultra 7 4870K and 4850K chips. Both will reportedly have a 125-watt power rating and 24 cores, but will again differ in terms of L3 cache — the former will have 144 MB, the latter just 36 MB. Both will boost to 5.2 GHz.

The report says the entry-level models will include the Core Ultra 5 4650K and 4650KF, both packing 22 cores and 30 MB L3 caches, and that they'll also have the same 125-watt power rating and top out at a boosted 5.1 GHz, according to the documentation.

A while ago, we reported that NVIDIA is reportedly cutting its gaming and consumer GPU supply by as much as 20-30%. NVIDIA is set to prioritize the AI GPU supply, which may result in a delayed RTX 6000 series launch, meaning the RTX 50 series will be around for a long time. The effect of such decisions is already pushing even the budget GPUs beyond affordability, and the latest data from Gazlog highlights a staggering price jump for some of the RTX 50 SKUs.

The GeForce RTX 5070, which launched at $549 in the NA region and for about 108,800 Yen in Japan last year, is now touching the $900 mark. In Japan, the lowest price for the card recorded on July 28th was reportedly 103,800 Yen or US$651. However, in just four months, the lowest price rose to nearly 149,800 yen, or US$940. Keep in mind that we aren't talking about the average RTX 5070 price here, but the cheapest RTX 5070 you will find in the Japanese market.

This marks a staggering 44% price increase in just four months. If you take a look at some regular RTX 5070 listings on some Japanese retailers, you will find many models selling for around 170,000-200,000 yen, which is roughly US$1000-US$1250. So, the average selling price might be closer to $1000 or may be even higher. For comparison, the RTX 5080 Founders Edition was launched at $999, and the significantly slower GPU with 4 GB less VRAM now sells for more.

We also checked the RTX 5070 prices in other regions and found a dramatic price increase as well. In the US, the cheapest RTX 5070 you can find costs nearly $900. On Amazon US, it's the MSI RTX 5070 12G Ventus 2X OC, which sells at $899, while Newegg has the GIGABYTE WindForce RTX 5070 as the cheapest card with an $899 price tag.

While there has already been plenty of back-and-forth over Anthropic’s compute relationship with SpaceX, a brief note from SemiAnalysis’s institutional desk has just raised fresh uncertainty —compounded by SpaceX’s reported decision to slash its GPU rental prices.

SpaceX’s compute ambitions are in flux amid Anthropic contract uncertainty

Earlier in November, we reported on a recent meeting between Anthropic's executives and sell-side analysts, where the former bluntly stated that the AI lab's compute deal with SpaceX would not be extended beyond the middle of next year, or Q2 2027.

Those reports then prompted a nonchalant response from Elon Musk, who said SpaceX "would be happy to take the compute back," while adding that "the opposite is going to happen."

Last week, Elon Musk took another jab at these reports, declaring:

"I think that it’s unlikely that they will do so. When I’ve talked to Anthropic, they tell me it is extremely likely that they will continue to rent compute from SpaceX, and in fact, that they want significantly more."

"But they have to say, like, in a worst-case scenario where there are extreme curtailments placed on what AI or SI can do, then they may not be able to use compute."

"But they’ve told me that their sort of highest probability outcome is that they would like an incremental 10 gigawatts of compute from SpaceX. So that’s a big number."

However, according to a note from SemiAnalysis's institutional desk that is currently circulating in both Chinese- and English-speaking circles, Anthropic might not renew its contract with SpaceX for a cluster of around 50,000 H200 GPUs.

For the benefit of those who might not be aware, from December 2026 onward, Anthropic is already slated to pay SpaceX $3.1 billion per month for renting its compute. Do note that Elon Musk's space- and AI-focused enterprise earned nearly a third of its revenue from Anthropic in Q3 2026, and stands to earn $120.5 billion cumulatively through FY 2029 under the current deal structure.

Coming back, the note asserts that SpaceX has already begun offering this compute capacity to other customers, with availability expected as soon as early 2027 and a quoted price of about $5 per GPU-hour.

To make matters worse, SpaceX has also reportedly slashed its Blackwell GPU spot quote for small compute clusters from about $15.0–$15.5 per GPU-hour to $10–$12, aligning these rates with its quotes for large-scale clusters already serving major customers such as Anthropic and Google.

SpaceX's reduction in spot compute rental prices signals that the GPU scarcity premium is finally beginning to fade. Even so, the note reiterates key assumptions in SemiAnalysis's valuation model, including a baseline of about $50 million per IT megawatt per year for GB300 capacity —equivalent to roughly $12 per GPU-hour.

This comes amid a glut of compute capacity, especially in Asia, after the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) recently introduced an interim final rule mandating licenses for advanced AI chips and servers shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil.

articles.title: Resourceful PC owner repurposes CPU watercooler with dead pump as standalone LCD hardware monitor, vibecodes new software for module
articles.summary: The Redditor salvaged the LCD and controller board, 3D-printed a stand, and used AI to develop a custom software to turn the screen into a standalone PC monitoring display.
articles.content_html:
Resourceful PC owner repurposes CPU watercooler with dead pump as standalone LCD hardware monitor, vibecodes new software for module — NZXT Kraken’s LCD and controller board combined with 3D-printed stand for second chance at life

News

Kunal Khullar

A clever way to save a dead cooler's LCD.

2

Follow us

AIO liquid coolers are notorious for shorter lifespans due to pump failure or leaks, which usually results in having to replace the entire unit. However, one enthusiast decided to salvage theirs uniquely, at least a part of it. Sharing their DIY project on Reddit, u/BodeeHav repurposed the LCD screen from a dead NZXT Kraken AIO into a standalone desktop monitor that displays live CPU and GPU temperatures and utilization after vibecoding entirely new software.

According to the post, the pump on their NZXT Kraken AIO stopped working around a month ago. Rather than discarding a perfectly usable screen, they decided to dismantle the block and remove the LCD and its main board. They used the original black outer housing and 3D printed a stand to hold the LCD in place. To keep things tidy, they stripped the connector down to just its SATA power and USB pins. The display connects directly to the motherboard, presumably using the internal 9-pin USB header, although BodeeHav says they plan to adapt it for external USB.

Repurposed my dead NZXT Kraken AIO screen into a desktop temp monitorr/pcmasterrace

Getting the display working properly required more than just pulling it out of the pump block. BodeeHav initially used NZXT’s CAM software; however, he kept running into issues whenever the PC entered sleep or standby. To overcome this hurdle, they turned to AI and vibe coded an entirely new software as a replacement that offers full control of the LCD with various customization options.

BodeeHav has graciously made his entire project available on GitHub, where you can access the DesktopKraken software and an STL file for the stand. According to the official GitHub page, the software is a standalone Windows application that communicates with compatible NZXT Kraken Elite LCDs over USB without requiring NZXT CAM.

The software currently only offers support for the 2023 Kraken Elite and 2024 Kraken Elite V2, which use circular LCDs with a 640x640 resolution. Apart from CPU and GPU temperatures and utilization, it can also display clock speeds, power consumption, memory usage, and VRAM information. Additionally, the software can be used for brightness control, screen orientation, sensor logging, and it even offers support for custom images, animated GIFs, thermal warning gauges, and automatic recovery after Windows sleep or a USB disconnect.

While it may cater to a very niche audience, the project is a great example of how a little ingenuity can give failed components a second life.

articles.content_html:
To scale large, open, dynamic worlds with ray tracing, AMD is developing a new approach to simplify the process. By extending traditional techniques, AMD introduces Ray Tracing Multi-Level Acceleration Structures (RT-MLAS). This technology adds additional levels of reusable acceleration structures within ray-traced objects, reducing both memory consumption and the time required to build and update them. Traditional ray tracing pipelines rely on two levels of acceleration structures: Bottom-Level Acceleration Structures (BLAS), which contain geometry, and a Top-Level Acceleration Structure (TLAS), which organizes instances of that geometry. However, large open worlds can have an enormous number of objects, making the TLAS increasingly expensive to rebuild as objects move or change their level of detail (LOD).

RT-MLAS addresses this challenge by introducing Mid-Level Acceleration Structures (MDLAS), allowing developers to organize objects into additional reusable hierarchies. AMD's implementation supports up to two additional levels, enabling repeated scene components to share acceleration structures rather than being individually duplicated or registered in an increasingly large TLAS. For example, an entire building can be represented by an MDLAS containing reusable walls, windows, doors, and roof components. This approach is particularly useful for open-world environments, where developers can organize different areas into independently manageable structures and rebuild only the sections that need updating. AMD's research also shows how the technology can benefit heavily animated environments, such as forests with tens of thousands of independently animated plants.

The newly leaked spec sheet details crucial information on the upcoming Intel Nova Lake-S processors, including the 28-core bLLC variant.

Two Nova Lake-S Chips Get 144 MB LLC Cache While the Third BFC Variant Sticks With 120 MB, Reveals Leaked Document With Seven Nova Lake-S SKUs

We have been reporting on the Nova Lake-S for months now, and we previously published posts detailing some of the high-end SKUs in the lineup. Our coverage mostly included the Intel Core Ultra 9 4970K and the Core Ultra 7 4870K, which are among the handful of bLLC variants with additional cache, aimed at competing against AMD's X3D chips.

We also reported on one or two more SKUs, like the Intel Core Ultra 5 4650K, and the latest report confirms the previously reported specifications. Thanks to Videocardz for getting their hands on the Intel document that contained information on seven Nova Lake-S desktop processors. The outlet claims that the document listed CPUs based on the C1 stepping qualification samples, and it's likely that the final products will arrive with the mentioned specifications.

According to the document, the Intel Core Ultra 9 4970K BFC 28-core variant will get 144 MB of LLC (Last Level Cache), and the other one with the same cache size will be the Intel Core Ultra 7 4870K BFC. Only the Core Ultra 9 4900 BFC will have a slightly reduced LLC cache of 120 MB. However, it's a low-power variant with a 65W TDP rating. The rest of the stack has a default TDP rating of 125W.

articles.title: The state of China's memory industry in 2026
articles.summary: China's memory output comes from CXMT and YMTC, a few smaller fabs, and Chinese Samsung and SK hynix plants, but no Chinese maker has HBM in volume yet.
articles.content_html:
The state of China's memory industry in 2026 — CXMT and YMTC are booming, but HBM remains a headache

Features

Shane Downing

A record year for Chinese memory, while Huawei ships its own HBM without a named source.

Follow us

China’s homegrown memory comes largely from two companies, CXMT for DRAM and YMTC for 3D NAND, and both are booming. CXMT’s Oct. 30 quarterly report shows a nine-month net profit of ¥132.0 billion ($19.6 billion), against a ¥5.28 billion ($785 million) loss a year earlier, on revenue more than eight times as high, at ¥269.0 billion ($40.0 billion). YMTC’s numbers, just for Q1, are at ¥47.04 billion ($7.0 billion) in revenue and ¥33.38 billion ($5.0 billion) in profit attributable to shareholders, more than double 2025.

Both are expanding and adding fabs, and each is edging into the other’s products. No Chinese manufacturer can yet produce high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in volume, though. HBM is the stacked DRAM that AI accelerators depend on, and currently the U.S. bars Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron from selling it into China. CXMT’s prospectus lists no HBM project, though its HBM3E is reportedly in risk production, an early run before the process is fully qualified. Huawei designs its own HBM but doesn’t say who makes it.

Memory is a commodity, so the story is in the wafers. We cover the companies running memory fabs in China: CXMT, YMTC, a handful of smaller Chinese fabs, and Samsung and SK hynix, which run some of their biggest plants there. Huawei makes the cut for its HBM program, though it has no memory fab. Fabless designers, module makers, and NOR flash producers are left out, except XMC for its HBM line. Fab counts, products, and financials come from filings and company statements; capacities, planned fabs, and the HBM progress that remains the big question mark rest largely on anonymous reporting. Let's dive into the current state of the Chinese DRAM industry.

CXMT: three DRAM fabs running, three more on the way

CXMT, short for ChangXin Memory Technologies, is China’s biggest homegrown DRAM maker. It operates two 12-inch fabs in Hefei and one in Beijing, each able to produce around 100,000 wafers a month. It is also building fabs in Shanghai and Hefei and is in funding talks for a second Beijing fab, which together could take it past 600,000 wafers a month. The Shanghai fab is expected to have two to three times the capacity of the Hefei base, with tools going in during the second half of 2026 and volume in 2027.

CXMT is now the fourth-largest DRAM maker worldwide, with 9.5% of DRAM revenue in Q2, according to TrendForce. CXMT says LPDDR6 is in mass production for Xiaomi, and its president says the first 4F² product, a server DDR5 RDIMM, is due by year-end. This comes after record first-half revenue of ¥150.3 billion ($22.4 billion), net profit of ¥77.6 billion ($11.5 billion), an 84.84% gross margin on its main business, and a listing on Shanghai’s STAR Market on July 27. Third-quarter profit alone was ¥54.4 billion ($8.1 billion).

The primary products are DDR5 rated up to 8,000 MT/s with 24Gb dies, and LPDDR5X rated up to 10,667 MT/s. CXMT says its fifth-generation G5 platform reaches 11.95nm active-area half-pitch with quadruple patterning for 24Gb LPDDR5X, and gets at least 50% more dies out of each wafer than G4, counted as 8Gb dies. CXMT says a DRAM product on its sixth-generation platform has also completed engineering-sample validation. Jeongdong Choe, Senior Technology Fellow at TechInsights, told Tom’s Hardware Premium that the firm measured the smallest active half-pitch on CXMT’s G4 at 14.8nm and hasn’t analyzed G5 yet.

CXMT lists no GDDR or 3D NAND among its products and is limited to nodes made without extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography as it lacks the tooling. CXMT’s second Beijing fab, however, is planned to include a 3D NAND R&D line, which could shake things up. The growth picture for now is capacity and price, with the tests of scaling without EUV lying with the RDIMM and Shanghai fab.

YMTC: going all out on NAND, DRAM in testing

YMTC, short for Yangtze Memory Technologies Co., has two fabs of its own in Wuhan, which can produce about 200,000 wafers a month together. A third fab in the Xinzhou district, registered in September last year, is expected to produce about 50,000 wafers a month by 2027 and eventually 100,000 at full capacity. While YMTC is known for its NAND flash, roughly half of Fab 3’s output is earmarked for DRAM. The company also makes enterprise SSDs and UFS and eMMC parts, and sells consumer SSDs under its ZhiTai brand. YMTC filed its own STAR Market prospectus, to match CXMT’s, on Aug. 21.

NAND flash was, until recently, the star of the show for Chinese memory, and YMTC’s Xtacking technology is one reason why. Its fifth-generation Xtacking 4.0 die, used in 1Tb TLC and 2Tb QLC parts, has 294 gates, and Choe told us 267 of them are active word lines. Most of what YMTC ships, however, is still 160- and 232-layer NAND. Samsung licensed YMTC’s Xtacking bonding patents in February 2025, so the technology could be considered both proven and valuable.

Omdia data put YMTC at 38.5% of China’s NAND market in Q2, ahead of Samsung’s 33.5%. Globally, YMTC ranked third in NAND shipments in Q2, according to Counterpoint Research, and its share of NAND revenue rose from 9% to 14% between Q1 2025 and Q1 2026. YMTC’s stated long-term targets are about 20% of global NAND supply and about 500,000 wafers a month, DRAM included.

For DRAM, YMTC’s Fab 2 is running about 5,000 wafers a month of 16Gb LPDDR5, still in R&D and testing, with no plan for mass production. However, a 9,600 MT/s part on a vertical channel transistor (VCT) 4F² cell is slated for mass production at Fab 3 if it passes qualification. XMC, YMTC’s former foundry unit, left its control in July.

The smaller fabs: Jinhua’s DDR4 and SwaySure’s unfinished line

Two smaller fabs worthy of note are Fujian Jinhua and SwaySure. The former has a 12-inch fab in Jinjiang, which produces custom DDR4 on 25nm, at 40,000–50,000 wafers a month, with about 90% going to Huawei. DDR4 prices have surged this year, by as much as 50% in the first quarter alone, as the big suppliers wind DDR4 down in favor of server and HBM parts and enterprise buyers stock up.

SwaySure, a Shenzhen company founded in March 2022 with state-owned investment, is building a 28nm 12-inch DRAM line and is reportedly backed by Huawei. Analyst Jim Handy of Objective Analysis doubts the 28nm line could make HBM. Neither company responded to our requests for additional information.

HBM: who’s chasing, and who isn’t

Not every AI chip needs HBM. Inference hardware can get by on LPDDR5X, as Axera’s AX8860P does in Sipeed’s MaixStation, or on DRAM bonded straight onto the processor, the approach PieceMakers is betting on. Training-class accelerators like Huawei’s Ascend series still need HBM, though, and since the U.S. banned the export of HBM as of Dec. 2, 2024, China can’t buy it from the big three memory makers.

Even those who can get HBM are seeing heat and yield issues with larger memory stacks, specifically 12-high. SK hynix said on its Q3 2026 earnings call that some customers’ spec changes show “demand is indeed overwhelming supply,” and that lowering the stack is “a strategy to increase the number of cubes that can be obtained for the same capacity.” This mirrors other indicators, including potential Nvidia Rubin Ultra decisions, and it suggests that HBM is in short enough supply that even easier-to-build stacks are in high demand.

CXMT has sampled HBM with Tongfu, and HBM3 built on its 16nm-class G4 node to Huawei. Its HBM3E has now gone to several domestic AI chip designers as samples, with limited production due by the end of 2026, and an expansion expected in 2027. Yields are only about 20% to 30%, though, against about 70% at SK hynix, and in testing the chips performed closer to SK hynix’s HBM3 than to its HBM3E. An HBM packaging plant in Shanghai worth at least ¥17.1 billion ($2.5 billion) is targeted for year-end, with capacity for about 30,000 units a month.

Tongfu reportedly sampled HBM2, but its own filings mention only DRAM and flash packaging. Huawei said last year that “we will offer two proprietary HBMs.” It launched the Atlas 350 card in March, built on the Ascend 950PR, which carries 112GB of HBM. XMC has had a 3,000-wafer-a-month HBM line under construction since early 2024, but no production has been confirmed. At this time, YMTC, Jinhua, and SwaySure don’t appear to make HBM, though reports say YMTC is developing the through-silicon via (TSV) stacking it would need, and Jinhua was named in a Huawei-led HBM group in 2024.

Huawei said in 2025 that the 950PR would use HiBL 1.0, its own “low-cost HBM”; TechInsights told us it hasn’t analyzed HiBL 1.0 yet. However, Huawei’s 2025 roadmap specced out the 950PR's 128GB of HBM at 1.6TB/s. Huawei said that its 950PR is “optimized for the prefill stage of inference,” which is compute-heavy with “lower demand for memory access bandwidth,” and that using HiBL 1.0 is “more cost-effective than HBM3E and HBM4E” for that workload. The higher-end HiZQ 2.0, for the 950DT, is due in Q4 and, by Huawei’s figures, brings 144GB at 4TB/s. In both cases, Huawei’s supplier remains in doubt, and the company did not respond to our requests for comment.

The foreign fabs, and the restrictive rules

Of the companies from outside China, Samsung and SK hynix both run large memory fabs on Chinese soil, and both are now upgrading their NAND lines there. Samsung’s Xi’an handles about 40% of the company’s NAND, including 236-layer, or V8, in volume, with X2 converting to 286-layer, or V9, this year, slated to reach 5,000 V9 wafers a month in December and 40,000 by December 2027. A Samsung spokesperson told Tom’s Hardware Premium that the company “has been transitioning its existing manufacturing operations in Xi’an to 9th-generation V-NAND in compliance with U.S. export regulations and in close communication with the U.S. government.”

SK hynix’s Wuxi produces 30–40% of its DRAM and has moved from 1z to 1a, with the EUV layers done in Korea. Dalian turns out about 100,000 wafers a month of 192-layer floating-gate NAND and is moving to 240 layers, the most SK hynix is authorized to make there.

SK hynix, which already sells NAND with up to 321 layers elsewhere, told us it needs a U.S. license every year and declined to give product details or capacities for individual fabs. The company said that it intends for its 321-layer flash to be “over 50% of domestic (Korean) capacity in the fourth quarter,” which puts the Dalian lag into relief.

SK hynix also has “Mod B,” a second fab at its Dalian site that was completed in 2023. The company has reportedly tied a new U.S. NAND fab to Washington, letting it ship more U.S. tools there: Dalian’s 2026 license capped its equipment, no 2027 license had been issued as of mid-October, and its U.S.-based Solidigm unit has applied for an export license to buy more tools for Mod B. SK hynix told Tom’s Hardware that “no capacity expansion is being sought for the Dalian Mod B” and has been installing equipment at its Dalian factory.

Solidigm is now reportedly in talks with the U.S. Commerce Department over a $45 billion chip plant in the U.S., but wants Washington’s approval to ship equipment to upgrade the Dalian plant first, arguing that the upgrade would help finance the new site. However, SK hynix denied an earlier report of such a deal and says no specific plans have been finalized.

As for its Chongqing packaging plant, SK hynix told us it is “exploring various strategic options to enhance our packaging competitiveness,” though nothing is final. Elsewhere in China, Samsung’s Suzhou plant handles assembly and testing, and Micron’s Xi’an site handles packaging and testing.

All of this plays out inside a U.S.-China fight over chips that AI has only sped up. CXMT isn’t currently on the Commerce Department’s Entity List, which bars U.S. suppliers from shipping to listed companies without a license; YMTC, Jinhua, and SwaySure are. Jinhua has been on the list since 2018; SwaySure joined in December 2024 over its Huawei links, and YMTC was added in December 2022.

CXMT is, however, on the Pentagon’s 1260H list of Chinese military companies, which it is suing over. It’s been on the list since January 2025 and stayed on with the June update. For Samsung and SK hynix, the validated end-user status that let both firms ship in U.S. tools was revoked as of Dec. 31, 2025. Annual licenses are now required, and the Commerce Department has said it doesn’t intend to license capacity expansions or technology upgrades. Meanwhile, both companies say upgrades are under way, which sits uneasily with that policy.

China, for its part, has been weighing broader technology export controls and has now proposed adding 40 technologies, reportedly including some memory-chip design technologies, to its Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited and Restricted from Export. The draft, Announcement 48 from China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology, is open for comment until Nov. 15, and anyone exporting a listed technology must register first.

articles.title: Google DeepMind AI engineers conjure mathematical proof of Signal's encryption protocol
articles.summary: Google DeepMind AI engineers conjure mathematical proof of Signal's encryption protocol — AlphaProof Code framework powered human-bot cooperation for speedy work
articles.content_html:
Google DeepMind AI engineers conjure mathematical proof of Signal's encryption protocol — AlphaProof Code framework powered human-bot cooperation for speedy work

News-analysis

Bruno Ferreira

Code tests are one thing, but a mathematical proof is one heck of a security blanket.

Follow us

A team at Google's DeepMind AI labs has performed a complete formal proof of the code that implements the encryption mechanism for the Signal private chat application. The scientists call their procedure AlphaProof Code and claim it can be applied to other situations requiring complete end-to-end verification of computer code, meaning Signal is safe, and you can find the full paper and the code repository detailing the proof.

More explicitly, the team reviewed an Arm-compiled version of libsignal, the library that the Signal application itself incorporates and uses, with some minimal scaffolding around it. Note that the verification wasn't done against the source code: it was purposely executed against an AArch64 binary, meaning the method can be reused for future verifications of other software.

In a similar vein to the AI labs' work on mathematics, the bulk of the work was done in Lean, a purpose-built language for formal proofs. There's a key difference for this effort, though. Lean is primarily used to prove the underlying math in algorithms, which in this case would be the specifications for Signal's encryption.

However, what the scientists actually did was create millions of lines of Lean proofs that were run against the actual implementation, in this case checking that the final binary executable corresponds to the initial specification.

Everyone knows about code tests in software development, but a mathematical proof of code is a different beast altogether, and one particularly elusive over the history of computing. It's akin to being able to check that an entire factory campus produces the actual parts it was designed to make, with the same exact inputs, with zero variation, no matter what else is happening.

The DeepMind scientists mention previous year-long efforts in this vein to create formal proofs for relatively small pieces of software. The seL4 microkernel purportedly took twenty years to prove, while CompCert's C compiler took six. This may sound like going way overboard on software engineering, until you consider that said programs are now, in practical terms, bulletproof and cannot fail due to a code flaw, at least for the inputs they control.

While it'd be a questionable use of resources to formally prove all software on Earth, AlphaProof Code providing the ability to do so for mission-critical code like the Signal comms protocol is quite a boon.

As an oversimplification, the actual AlphaProof Code workflow comprised various stages of back-and-forth between humans and Gemini 4 Carbon agents. The first steps were laying out the groundwork and infrastructure. The team defined the base scope of work, and then created textual bot skills to prepare agents for their future tasks, among them specification writers, proof workers, and orchestration.

Then, it was time to have agents create the first set of Lean definitions for AArch64 instructions, how registers, memory, and system calls work, and how Linux processes operate. At this point, however, nothing is proven about Signal or any other application. That came next, as the team and its army of agents drafted fully revised specifications for libsignal's cryptography implementation. This then generated just over 1.2 million lines of Lean, for checking the mathematical reasoning behind the protocol.

The bulk of the agentic work was generating 5.3 million lines of Lean to verify that each binary instruction matched the previously defined AArch64, CPU, and process formal behaviors. During this stage, the agent flagged one percent of the codebase for humans to review and verify. When it was all complete, the team had fully verified that the cryptographic engine in the binary did indeed match all the generated proofs, down to the last processed bit.

As the researchers point out: "the most important lesson from our experience is that, once proofs become cheap, the hard question is what to prove," adding that "the majority of our effort went not into proofs but into specifications," and underscoring that this is particularly important for software topics like cryptography.

Interestingly, they mention that "writing specifications against real code also turned out to be a stress test for the literature," an insightful note on verifying that one did write the software's specifications properly to begin with.

With the disclaimer that this is a note about security in general and we think Signal is indeed top-notch as a private messaging application: Google's team "only" proved that libsignal works exactly as advertised. If a malicious actor were to booby-trap the Signal app — or any other one — with additional code to copy your messages, this sort of proof likely wouldn't catch it. Likewise, the fact that a third-party app implements the Signal protocol for encryption doesn't automatically mean it offers full privacy.

articles.content_html:
Grand Theft Auto VI runs better on Xbox Series X than on PlayStation 5, reveals Digital Foundry, thus essentially defeating Sony's narrative that the game plays best on PS5.

In the full technical comparison of the various consoles, DF's Oliver Mackenzie notes that Grand Theft Auto VI's frame rate dips more on PS5:

In typical play, both hit 30 FPS or don't fall far below, but Grand Theft Auto VI is balanced on a knife's edge in performance terms, and the game can dip below 30 FPS more often than I'd like. PS5 seems substantially worse off in this respect. I managed to roughly match a few sequences, and PS5 drops frames more often than Series X in spots that seem to cause issues for this game, like in fast vehicle traversal. Often with PS5 and Series X releases, we spot minor resolution differences that favor Series X, but GTA seems to operate with matching settings on both consoles, and I suspect that is hurting PS5 with its smaller GPU. The PS5's lower CPU clock could also hurt the game depending on the scene and load. In most games, these minor performance differences wouldn't be obvious. Grand Theft Auto VI is seemingly set up to exhibit these differences in a very obvious way. GTA VI on PS5 doesn't support 120 Hz VR either, so Xbox gets an easy win there, helping to mitigate any performance drops that pop up. Dips to the upper 20s seem harder to notice on Xbox with this enabled. Overall performance on PS5 and Series X is fine, but Series X seems to have a small, noticeable edge in similar content. Microsoft's machine is meaningfully better off than the PS5 in this game, which is a little surprising.

Honestly, I wouldn't say it's that surprising. We always knew the Xbox Series X was the more capable machine of the two, thanks to its higher number of Compute Units (52 versus 36), which yield a Teraflop count of 12.155, compared to the PS5's 10.28. The CPU is also slightly higher clocked (3.8 GHz, while the PS5 stops at 3.5 GHz). Perhaps it is more surprising that few games have shown a meaningful advantage for the Xbox Series X.

Of course, I'd argue the PS5 definitely offers a better experience when it comes to immersion thanks to its superior DualSense controller, whose controller speaker, haptic feedback, and adaptive triggers combine to meaningfully enhance the player's connection with Leonida. And the PS5 Pro is most assuredly the best way to play Grand Theft Auto VI, at least until it comes out on PC, providing better image quality and a more stable frame rate.

Still, the Xbox consoles fared well, with the Series X's advantage over the PS5 and the Xbox Series S punching above its weight with the first-ever implementation of AMD FSR 4 on the platform, as revealed exclusively by Wccftech.

In other Grand Theft Auto VI news, Sensor Tower has shared its updated sales estimates for the game as of Sunday, November 22, and they're even higher than Alinea's. According to Sensor Tower, GTA VI sold 47.8 million units by the end of the launch weekend, with more than a third (35%) of active consoles installing the game. Like Alinea, the analyst firm points to big declines for Call of Duty and Fortnite, but adds that even Crimson Desert and 007 First Light saw their daily active users dwindle by 33% and 27%, respectively.

articles.title: AMD's Radeon RX 9060 XT sets new GPU frequency world record of 4.837 GHz
articles.summary: AMD's Radeon RX 9060 XT has reached a new GPU frequency world record of 4,837 MHz. AMD VP Jack Huynh and veteran overclocker Bill Alverson used liquid nitrogen cooling to help the smaller RDNA 4 GPU open a 48MHz gap over the previous world record run.
articles.content_html:
Radeon RX 9060 XT sets new GPU frequency world record of 4.837 GHz — AMD overclocking team pushes mid-range RDNA 4 GPU to the max under liquid nitrogen

News

Kunal Khullar

AMD's smaller RDNA 4 GPU gets one step closer to 5 GHz.

1

Follow us

AMD has set a new GPU overclocking world record by pushing the Radeon RX 9060 XT to 4,837 MHz. Veteran overclocker Bill Alverson and AMD VP Jack Huynh found the limits of this particular chip as part of a celebration of the opening of a new Micro Center location in Austin, Texas. According to the OC World Record Museum database maintained by SkatterBencher, Huynh and Alverson set the new record on November 15.

If you were expecting to see this record from AMD's high-end RX 9070 XT, you're not crazy. The record was indeed achieved using the midrange RDNA 4 part rather than AMD’s flagship GPU. The RX 9060 XT uses a smaller Navi 44 GPU featuring 2,048 shading units (32 compute units), a 160W TDP, 16GB of GDDR6 memory on a 128-bit bus, and a stock boost clock speed of up to 3,130 MHz.

A NEW @microcenter in Austin. An INCREDIBLE community. And a GPU WORLD RECORD. I had an absolute blast celebrating with Austin's gamers, PC builders, and creators. From meeting fans and snapping photos to building PCs and sharing our passion for all things tech. And then came an even BIGGER moment... I joined forces with Bill Alverson and our @AMD overclocking team. Armed with liquid nitrogen and pushing frequencies to the absolute limit, we set our sights on something BIG: breaking the GPU FREQUENCY WORLD RECORD! And we did it! 4.837 GHz! And we captured the whole thing on camera, including the moment we broke the record! Epic energy. Epic builds. WORLD RECORDS!November 24, 2026

The new frequency record was achieved using liquid nitrogen cooling. At 4,837 MHz, the GPU was running approximately 54.5% faster than its advertised boost frequency. A GPU-Z screenshot confirms the record breaking frequency with the GPU temperature at -49°C, 62W power draw, and voltage at 1.434V.

Of course, nobody should expect these numbers to bear any relationship to the clock speeds that can be achieved from any stock, air-cooled RX 9060 XT. Liquid nitrogen and liquid helium are commonly used in extreme overclocking, as they bring component temperatures well below what air and liquid cooling at ambient temperatures can achieve, essentially removing thermal limits from an overclocking attempt and enabling large amounts of power to be pushed into a chip for the highest clocks.

But these coolants require careful preparation of hardware, constant monitoring, and custom heatsinks to contain them while an extreme overclocking run is in progress, and they're only useful for short durations due to evaporation.

Such record-breaking frequencies are primarily intended to demonstrate the absolute limits of the hardware itself, rather than serve as an example of sustained performance for everyday use cases.

This isn’t the first time enthusiasts have pushed AMD’s RDNA 4 GPU to extreme frequencies. The RX 9060 XT previously reached 4,769 MHz in February 2026, followed by another attempt in June which reportedly reached 4,789 MHz. The latest attempt is 48 MHz higher compared to the previous record, bringing AMD’s latest GPU IP closer than ever to the elusive 5 GHz milestone.

For the average gamer, the biggest obstacle to getting the most out of an RX 9060 XT isn't its overclocking headroom, but its high price in late 2026. The RX 9060 XT 16GB had an MSRP of just $349, but these cards are currently selling for over $700, making this formerly budget-friendly enthusiast card a poor value today. Achieving a world-record GPU frequency on one of these chips is an impressive achievement in extreme overclocking, but it's unlikely to translate into more Radeon gamers any time soon.

There's a new CPU benchmark on the way designed to handle and contextualize 40 years of personal computer chip development. The upcoming CrystalMark CPUix "evaluates performance from i386 through the latest processors using a single standard across past and future CPU generations," says developer Noriyuki Miyazaki [machine translation]. In terms of hardware/software compatibility, the benchmarking tool will evaluate processors as old as the i386 running on OSes as out of date as Windows 95 and NT 3.51.

Windows 95/NT 3.51以降に対応し、i386から最新、さらに将来のCPUまで、 世代を超えて性能を一つの基準で評価する新世代CPUベンチマークソフト「CrystalMark CPUix」を鋭意企画中です。 CrystalMark CPUix Project Site https://t.co/OEjTdlr4bU https://t.co/ZAfjuz6sYtJuly 29, 2026

Miyazaki says that the upcoming CPUix app will support 16-color environments, which might help folks at the more ancient and creaky end of the PC retro hardware spectrum. Even this limited color UI will have a base maroon theme, as used in the announcement graphic.

The developer is also welcoming feature requests on social media. Don't ask for support for OSes earlier than Windows 95, though, as it has already been stated by Miyazaki that stretching compatibility to Windows 3.1 "is a bit much."

To aid in the development of CPUix, Miyazaki has recently acquired an NEC PC-98 21Bs. This lovely beige desktop arrived on the developer's desk on Sunday, but it has already been used to implement and verify CPUix's functionality on processors without an FPU. Other older systems have been purchased, including a Pentium 100, to ensure wide compatibility. More systems, old and new, are also going to be acquired for testing.

We don't have a lot of information on the inner workings of CPUix as yet. Aspects of the benchmark's test workloads, score weighting, and so on aren't shared on the official pages or social media postings we found. As CPUix comes from the developer of CrystalDiskMark, it looks like it could be a more ambitious version of the CrystalMark Retro 2.0.0 release, which we reported on last year. That also supported systems back to Windows 95/NT 3.51, and CPUs from the i386 era.

CPUix is still in development, and its release date is currently penciled in for March 31, 2027. It seems to have been revealed early, as Miyazaki celebrates the 28th anniversary of Crystal Dew World.

articles.content_html:
Samsung is reportedly planning to increase its NAND production capacity in China, but it's unfortunately not the kind of NAND flash that will benefit regular consumers directly. According to Seoul Economic Daily, citing industry sources, Samsung plans to make roughly five times as much V9 NAND flash at its second fab in Xi'an, China, by the end of 2027. Sources tell SED that the X2 fab currently produces about 10,000 300 mm wafers of the 286-layer V9 NAND per month, and the plan is to raise that figure to around 50,000. This extra output is, to the surprise of no one, aimed at enterprise SSDs for AI data centers. It's interesting that this report has surfaced when NAND spot prices have already started falling.

As for the exact plans, the report says that Samsung will build an electroplating line in X2's empty cleanroom space, move equipment in around February 2027, and finish the conversion by November 2027. Additionally, 20% to 30% of the fab's existing V6 line will also be switched to V9. Overall, this looks like a plan to mostly shift to denser NAND inside an existing fab, rather than a brand-new factory expansion. Samsung has previously denied claims of expanding production capacity, so this might be more of a reshuffle. Still, the numbers suggest that a lot more NAND flash will indeed be produced according to the new plans. It looks like Samsung is doubling down on denser NAND, while TrendForce expects NAND contract prices to decline in 2027.

articles.content_html:
Maxsun has introduced the MS-Terminator Z890-C WIFI, an ATX motherboard for Intel LGA1851 processors. The board measures 305 x 245 mm, has a 10+1+1 phase power delivery system, and an eight-layer PCB. The four DDR5 DIMM slots support up to 256 GB of memory with up to 8,800 MT/s (OC). Expansion options include one PCIe 5.0 x16 slot with support for x8/x8 or x8/x4/x4 lane bifurcation. Three additional PCIe 4.0 slots provide x4, x1, and x1 connectivity via its Intel Z890 chipset. For storage, the board offers four M.2 slots. One supports PCIe 5.0 x4 while the other three use PCIe 4.0 x4 interfaces. The board also has four SATA 6 Gbps ports and an SFF-8654 4i connector. The latter supports either PCIe 4.0 x4 or four additional SATA connections to connect U.2 and U.3 NVMe SSDs.

Networking is handled by a Realtek RTL8125D 2.5 GbE controller and a MediaTek MT7902 wireless module with Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.2. Audio comes from a Realtek ALC897 codec. The rear I/O panel includes one HDMI 2.1, one DisplayPort 1.4, eight USB-A 5 Gbps ports, an RJ45 Ethernet port, two Wi-Fi antenna connectors, and audio jacks. According to IT Home, the Maxsun MS-Terminator Z890-C WIFI is available in China for CNY 1,249, or approximately $187. The motherboard also appears on the company's global website, but international pricing and availability have not been announced.

There was much excitement when Intel's Panther Lake CPUs launched with the powerful new Arc B390 iGPUs, and although Linux gaming performance was impressive on those systems, it always takes time for mainstream distributions, like Ubuntu, to catch up to bleeding edge hardware. For Ubuntu, it seems as though the 26.10 update has taken a pretty substantial step towards taking full advantage of the Intel Core Ultra X7 358H and its B390 iGPU, according to recent tests by Phoronix.

According to the testing, CPU performance improvements in tasks like code compilation and CPU-based AI workflows were minimal—on the order of 1-2%—but the iGPU saw significant improvements in graphics benchmarks, scoring a 65% FPS improvement in the yquake2 Vulkan benchmark and a 15% improvement in the GravityMark 1.87 Vulkan ray tracing benchmark. There were also some marginal improvements in media encoding benchmarks, with 4K AV1 encoding in particular seeing an improvement of up to 24%. These tests were conducted on a Dell XPS 14 laptop, which has historically been a thermally constrained form factor, so devices with a higher thermal ceiling can likely expect to see more improvements on the graphics side of things.

Single-slot graphics cards are quite a rare sight nowadays, especially for the newest generations from NVIDIA and AMD. INNO3D's RTX 5060 Ti PRO is seemingly a great option for those buyers who want a single-slot GPU for their compact builds. However, it looks like Japanese buyers will have to pay a hefty 169,400 yen (roughly $1,060) for this particular model. That information comes from an ELSA ONLINE listing, which is the web store of INNO3D's Japanese partner, ELSA Japan. INNO3D put up the product page for this card around 3 months ago, but the price was not known at that time. For comparison, ELSA's dual-slot RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB cards cost around 20,000 yen ($125) less. What's more interesting is that even some RTX 5070 models in Japan cost less than the single-slot INNO3D variant, at least according to October data.

So what do buyers get for spending a cool $1,060 for a single-slot RTX 5060 Ti? The shroud is just 20 mm thick, and inside is a stock RTX 5060 Ti with 4,608 CUDA cores, a 2,572 MHz boost clock, and 16 GB of GDDR7 VRAM on a 128-bit bus. There's only a single 8-pin connector, and power is rated at 180 W. As for thermals, a vapor chamber and blower fan push the heat out through the bracket. The dimensions are 265 x 111 x 20 mm, so it still needs a full-height slot. This particular variant looks like it's aimed at multi-GPU workstations, but it can also be useful for small form factor builders. INNO3D has done some one-slot cards before, such as the RTX 5090 and RTX 5080 Frostbite Pro, but those relied on Alphacool water blocks instead.
