articles.title: ASUS Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700 Review
articles.summary: Today we are taking a look at ASUS's high-end Radeon AI inference card for workstations, the Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700. With 32GB of RAM and a $2000 price tag, the card is a highly affordable way to fill out a workstation for local AI inference The post ASUS Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700 Review appeared first on ServeTheHome .
articles.content_html:
While much of the attention in the market for AI inference has been focused on servers and datacenter-scale deployments, the heart and soul of the modern AI revolution started with video cards. And that is where it still beats on today, overshadowed by servers but still an important market segment overall.

Within the AMD ecosystem, the company has taken a very visible pivot in how it markets and categorizes its professional video cards. The Radeon Pro lineup, once the backbone of AMD’s workstation graphics efforts, has become the Radeon AI Pro lineup, and the backbone of AMD’s add-in video card/AI accelerator efforts. The flagship for this line, in turn, is the Radeon AI Pro R9700, a 32GB VRAM card that AMD and its partners are positioning as a more budget-friendly alternative to NVIDIA’s RTX PRO Blackwell lineup of workstation cards.

Today we are taking a look at one of those R9700 cards in the form of ASUS’s Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700. The sub-$2000 card have been heavily optimized for workstation use, balancing graphics needs and display outputs with the ability to fit up to four cards into a single system for larger AI workloads.

ASUS Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700 Hardware Overview

As AMD is not selling their own reference design workstation cards for this generation, it falls to AMD’s partners to sell the cards instead. Which is a production strategy that they are well-accustomed to on the consumer side of matters, but is a bit more unusual for a workstation card.

Notably, AMD has been keeping their Radeon Pro partners on a rather short leash with card designs. AMD is curating a very specific image for a very specific market here, not the least of which is the ability to install multiple cards in a single workstation. As a result, though AMD is not selling their reference card their partner cards are all quite similar in their high-level design as dual slot blowers, a form factor you will not readily find outside of workstation video cards these days.

That brings us to ASUS’s Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700. ASUS has long been a heavyweight in the world of video cards, so it is no surprise to see them jump on board producing a Radeon Pro card.

ASUS’s R9700 card is, in all practical application, exactly what you would expect from a workstation card given the form factor and the AMD’s constraints. This is a dual slot video card that follows the PCIe specifications to a T in terms of width and height, in order to ensure that it (and perhaps a few of its friends) can fit into a workstation chassis.

ASUS Turbo Radeon AI R9700 Specifications
CUs 64
AI Accelerators 128
GPU Boost Clockspeed 2.92GHz
Peak Matrix Throughput (FP8) 382.7 TFLOPS
Peak Vector Throughput (FP32) 47.8 TFLOPS
Memory 32GB GDDR6
Memory Bandwidth640GB/sec

(20Gbps x 256-bits)
ECC Yes (Linux Only)
Infinity Cache 64MB
I/O PCIe Gen5 x16
TBP 300W
Form Factor PCIe CEM (Air Cooled)
Dimensions 267 x 111 x 40 mm (10.5 x 4.4 x 1.6 in)
Architecture RDNA 4
GPU Navi 48

Under the hood, the card is powered by AMD’s Navi 48 GPU, which is the most powerful RDNA 4 GPU offered in this generation. The GPU offers 64 of AMD’s CUs, which in turn is comprised of a total of 4096 shading units for vector math and 128 AI accelerator cores for matrix operations.

With a peak clock speed of 2.92GHz, this gives the R9700 a peak matrix math throughput of 382.7 TFLOPS with dense FP8 math, or double that with sparsity. One of the key improvements in this generation of RDNA architecture is the addition of FP8 support, which not only further improves the compute throughput of the card, but it better aligns AMD’s hardware with the general trends in the industry towards lower precision weights, and fitting a large number of weights within a given amount of memory.

On that note, as is traditional for a workstation card, AMD and ASUS have packed the R9700 with as much memory as the card can handle. With Navi 48 sporting a 256-bit bus, the card has been equipped with 32GB of GDDR6 memory organized as 16 2Gbit chips in clamshell mode. Above all else, memory support is a key differentiator between AMD’s consumer and professional cards, so 32GB is something you will only find on the Radeon AI Pro cards.

The GDDR6 memory itself is clocked at 20Gbps, allowing for a total of 640GB/second of memory bandwidth for the card. Soft ECC is also available, though only under Linux (and even then, it has to be manually enabled). This allows for an extra degree of reliability for systems and racks based around the card.

Navi 48 itself is somewhere between a mid to high-end GPU as far as die size (357mm2) and transistor counts (53.9B) go, which makes it a bit of an oddity within AMD’s lineup as far as card progression is concerned. AMD did not produce a true high-end GPU this generation, and as a result the R9700 actually has less VRAM than the previous-generation 48GB Radeon Pro W7900. This means that it is a step back in terms of overall memory capacity, but AMD is looking to make up the difference with compute throughput, thanks in large part to the newer chip architecture.

One advantage of being a smaller chip, however, is that it keeps TDPs in check. AMD (and ASUS’s) Total Board Power figure for the card is just 300 Watts, which makes it relatively easy to keep a blower-style card cooled without a blowout on noise. This also means that even 4 cards in a system is not going to result in excessive power requirements, though it will certainly be pushing the limits of a single power supply.

ASUS Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700 Build and Design

As far as video card designs go, ASUS’s Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700 is a very typical dual slot blower design. With a need to ensure that the card can be installed in multiples together, ASUS has kept things tightly tuned to PCIe specifications, with a dual slot card measuring 10.5 inches long and 4.4 inches high.

Interestingly, the blower design here is open-backed, that is, the back side of the card has open vents so that the card can pull in air from both sides of the card.

The fan itself is a pretty typical blower design. According to ASUS they are using dual ball bearings here.

Taking a look at the rear of the card, we can better see the venting cut into the card’s PCB and its shroud. For that matter, we can also see that the card even has a shroud on its back side. As noted earlier, the 32GB of GDDR6 is organized in a clamshell configuration on the R9700, meaning that 8 chips are on the rear of the card and need to be protected and cooled, just as with all of the chips on the front side of the card.

Being that this is a workstation card, ASUS has also put some thought into their power connector placement. The Turbo R9700 uses an ATX 12V-2×6 connector, which has been placed on the rear of the card instead of the top, another workstation-centric design element that makes it easier to install multiple cards in a system. The 12V-2×6 connector is rated for up to 600W, so the 300W TBP R9700 is well within the cable’s limits.

Meanwhile, at the front of the card we find a not too subtle reminder that this is a video card, with 4 display outputs – the maximum number of displays the Navi 48 GPU can drive. ASUS has given their card a triple DisplayPort plus single HDMI port configuration. The DisplayPorts are all DisplayPort 2.1a, while the HDMI port supports HDMI 2.1b. Coupled with DSC, and the card can drive displays at up to 12K in resolution.

Otherwise, besides the display outputs, the rest of the front of the card is almost entirely vent cut-outs. 300W is still a lot of heat to expel from a blower card, so ASUS does not hold back here, and you can clearly see the fins from the heatsink running within the card.

With our hardware tour complete, let us take a look at the performance of the Turbo R9700

articles.content_html:
AMD has quietly released the AGESA ComboAM5 PI 1.3.0.1f Patch A, which primarily introduces a 1.4 V maximum core voltage limit for select Ryzen 8000-series processors. Motherboard manufacturers are starting to roll out BIOS updates that incorporate this change. Both ASUS and MSI have noted the restriction in their release notes for AM5 motherboards. MSI's MEG X870E GODLIKE X EDITION received BIOS version 2A36 on November 18, which includes AGESA ComboAM5 PI 1.3.0.1f Patch A. The changelog specifically mentions limiting the maximum vCore to 1.4 V for select AMD Ryzen 8000-series CPUs. The update also adds additional POST codes to improve visibility into memory training, making it easier to differentiate between normal initialization activity and a system that has stopped responding.

ASUS has documented the same changes in its latest beta BIOS releases for several AM5 motherboard families, including the X870, X670, B850, and B650 models. This covers its ROG Crosshair, ROG Strix, TUF Gaming, and ProArt product lines. The company also describes a new memory-training sequence where the motherboard's debug display counts from 00 to 09, advancing approximately once per second before resetting to 00 and continuing with the normal boot process. However, the main focus is on limiting the maximum vCore voltage for Ryzen 8000 series CPUs. If you are using an AMD system with Ryzen 8000 series desktop APUs, please check your vendor's BIOS updates.

articles.content_html:
Jetway has introduced the MTX-RYZ1 Mini-ITX industrial motherboard built around the Ryzen 7 PRO 8845HS. The AMD "Hawk Point" Zen 4 chip has 8 cores and 16 threads with a 3.8 GHz base clock, and it's aimed mostly at embedded systems and industrial applications. The two SO-DIMM slots support up to 96 GB of DDR5-5600, with both ECC and non-ECC modules supported. For storage, the motherboard has two SATA III ports and two M.2 2280 slots. The M.2 slots are running at PCIe 4.0 x4. A separate M.2 2230 E-key slot gives PCIe x1 and USB 2.0 for an optional wireless module. A single PCIe 4.0 x8 slot is available for expansion. Networking comes from two Intel I226-V 2.5 GbE controllers, each with its own RJ45 port. The board can drive up to four independent displays over DisplayPort, eDP and LVDS (Low-Voltage Differential Signaling). Some of these outputs share board space, though. DP0 is co-layout with eDP, and DP1 shares its layout with LVDS.

Since this board is targeting the industrial side, there are two configurable RS-232/422/485 serial ports and four more RS-232 connections via internal headers. It also features a 16-bit GPIO header, SMBus, four rear USB 3.2 Gen 1 ports and six USB 2.0 ports through internal headers. Audio is handled by a Realtek ALC897 codec. A programmable watchdog timer, Wake-on-LAN and TPM 2.0 support round out the feature list.

articles.content_html:
It's well known that Rockstar loves its Easter eggs, but this one might just be the best one yet. Apparently, there is a time-traveling Easter egg in GTA 6 that takes you back to the original Vice City from 2002. Australian YouTuber Memeio found the complex Easter egg and published a guide on how to solve it, unlocking a trip down memory lane straight to the Malibu Club in Vice City. The best part is that Rockstar kept the older Vice City vibe intact, as the graphics switch to PS2-style and the character models also change. Completing the experience gives players a Tommy Vercetti Hawaiian shirt and a motorbike from the 2002 classic.

The process is quite complex, and it apparently took Memeio three days to crack it. It would be best to watch Memeio's video guide for the exact steps, but in a nutshell, it involves performing a series of steps one after the other at 13 different power stations spread across the map. The clues spell out "LIFE IS PASSING ME BY," which is a famous Vice City cheat code that speeds up the in-game clock. Completing all the steps correctly and without using fast travel unlocks a literal portal that teleports Jason to the Malibu Club from 2002's Vice City. You also meet Kent Paul, voiced by the original artist Danny Dyer, again. To complete this puzzle successfully, you do need to reach Chapter 3 to gain access to the full map. It's certainly a very amusing nod to the original GTA Vice City, a fan favorite of the series.

articles.title: JEDEC Previews DDR6 Memory Standard: 2.35x More Bandwidth, 44% Narrower DIMMs
articles.summary: JEDEC has unveiled the first specifications for DDR6 memory. Targeting over twice the bandwidth of DDR5, and with DIMMs 44% smaller, DDR6 is slated to be the biggest change in generations to the server memory standard The post JEDEC Previews DDR6 Memory Standard: 2.35x More Bandwidth, 44% Narrower DIMMs appeared first on ServeTheHome .
articles.content_html:
It is hard to believe that it has already been over 6 years since DDR5 memory was launched, but now in the fall of 2026 it is already time to start talking about the next generation of server memory.

This past week the JEDEC Solid State Technology Association, the industry consortium responsible for developing the various memory standards (among other specifications) released a preview of the in-development DDR6 memory standard.

The next generation of the group’s mainline SDRAM memory standard, DDR6’s development has been known about for quite some time now. But, outside of the customary bandwidth improvements, it has not been clear what other changes the DDR6 specification may bring with it. Now, following JEDEC’s preview, we have our first official look at what some of the major features of the new specification will be – or at least, are expected to be based on the current development plans.

DDR6 Memory Standard Preview: Smaller DIMMs, Bigger Bandwidth

As always, the key improvement in a new generation of DDR memory is the amount of bandwidth available per DIMM. DDR6, in turn, is planned to be a major overhaul of DDR memory technology in this regard, as it is tackling the matter from both ends.

In regards to per-pin bitrates, the current plan calls for DDR6 to start at 12.8 GT/sec and eventually reach 14.4 GT/sec and higher. Currently, DDR5 tops out at 9.2 GT/sec, so at the top end this would represent an eventual 57% increase in per-pin bandwidth. Meanwhile looking at things on a contextual basis, the original DDR5 specification stopped at 6.4 GT/sec, so if DDR6 were to eventually end up on a similar long-term trajectory, then “beyond” could eventually extend well past 14.4 GT/sec.

Still, a 57% increase is not as much bandwidth as some customers would like to see, so the group is also planning to take the more radical step of changing the bit-width of a DIMM itself. Following nearly three decades of DIMMs being 64-bits wide, going back to the days of single data rate SDRAM, the group is proposing to make DIMMs even wider, moving to a 96-bit wide memory bus.

With 32 more data pins (DQ lines), a DDR6 DIMM would offer 50% more bandwidth at identical clockspeeds to a DDR5 DIMM. Or, combining the two improvements, a full DDR6-14400 DIMM would offer 172.8GB/sec of bandwidth, or 2.35x as much bandwidth as a DDR5-9200 DIMM does today (and more still compared to the DDR5-8000 DIMMs that the latest server platforms actually support).

The switch to a wider bus width for an individual DIMM will come with some significant ramifications for the rest of the standard as well, in part because of the changes that need to happen in order to enable those wider DIMMs. Key to this, DDR6 will be employing a pseudo-channel architecture that splits up the individual channels.

Unfortunately, JEDEC’s preview announcement does not clarify if and how this might interact with the sub-channel architecture that DDR5 currently employs, so we do not have enough information to definitively state how this compares to DDR5’s architecture in this regard. But broadly speaking, splitting up DIMMs into multiple channels is how the most recent version of the standard was able to raise bandwidth in light of DRAM core clockspeeds having long grown stagnant, and some kind of similar change has been expected for DDR6 as well.

Regardless, the specification is also doubling the number of memory banks on a DIMM, which by our reckoning should bring it up to 16 banks per group. This is another change that should further help DDR6 deliver data at those higher pin bitrates, as it affords more banks that can be used while the other banks are busy refreshing.

The change to the individual DIMM memory bus width will also bring with it some physical changes to DIMM designs – and more than you might be expecting. JEDEC will be introducing a more compact 74mm wide DIMM for DDR6, which on a relative basis is just a bit wider than a DDR5 SO-DIMM. According to the group, the change is being made to allow for systems with higher memory densities as, while routing small traces is bad enough, 16 channels of DDR5 DIMMs takes up an immense amount of physical space that there is no real work-around for with their 133mm module width.

Notably, the group’s announcement does not clarify whether they will keep the current DIMM width, which like the 64-bit memory bus has been with the standard since the earliest days. Though JEDEC is quick to note that they are working on multiple form factors, potentially including RDIMMs, UDIMMs, and even CAMMs – the latter of which was added to DDR5 as a mid-generation feature. In that respect, the denser 73mm form factor may end up as a premium option for RDIMMs, especially as a smaller connector combined with a wider memory bus would require some very small pins on the new compact form factor.

Meanwhile, it is interesting to see that, at present, there is no mention of SO-DIMMs at all. So the small laptop DIMM factor may very well be on its way out in favor of CAMMs (or soldiered memory) for all laptops.

On the other hand, the preview announcement mentions server needs front and center. JEDEC’s members are well-aware of the need for more memory in the data center, and this is something that the group is explicitly looking to tackle. In practice, this would seem to be aiming to deliver on all three major features that data center operators are after: smaller DIMMs, more memory bandwidth per DIMM, and higher capacities overall.

Speaking of which, besides allowing for more DIMMs in a given amount of space, the DDR6 specification will also be tackling the memory capacity matter from the other direction as well. As always, the latest standard is increasing the maximum supported die density, bringing it from 64 Gbit to 128 Gbit. At the same time, the spec will make some unspecified optimizations for die stacking to allow for higher capacity packages overall. At present, die stacked DRAM packages are far from brand new, but 3DS DIMMs are still relatively uncommon overall.

A bit more nebulous, the announcement also notes support for multiple ECC implementations. The current DDR5 standard has a single ECC standard at the DIMM level for transmission and overall DIMM reliability, as well as on-die ECC to protect/correct the individual cells. In the past year we have seen some proposals for layering additional soft ECC on top of this to further improve reliability (e.g. Astera Labs’ Leo CXL memory expanders), so it may be that JEDEC is eyeing something similar, to let customers allocate additional DRAM capacity to storing ECC data for even higher levels of reliability.

Finally, the DDR6 standard will be taking steps to rein in the power consumption of DIMMs, which has been a concern with every generation as increased performance comes will otherwise drive up the power needs. For the next version of the spec, DDR6 will be switching to VSS-terminated I/O, as opposed to DDR5’s VDDQ-based termination – in effect terminating with a low voltage instead of a high voltage. The spec will also introduce low power modes for data center use, though the initial announcement does not go into further detail. Regardless, the consortium is targeting “significantly improved performance-per-watt” versus DDR5, which would be welcome across the board, but especially in data centers where power is a constraining factor and large DIMM counts are eating up larger amounts of that budget.

Final Words

Wrapping things up, JEDEC’s initial announcement for DDR6 emphasizes how the group has significant plans for the next generation of the memory standard. While it is true that every generation of DDR has been faster and lower power than the previous, how this is accomplished has changed with every generation – and it gets harder all the time. Meanwhile the physical DIMM changes are even more remarkable, and they underscore how the group is ready to break away from the form factors that have defined SDRAM for almost the last 30 years.

The net impact of these changes, in turn, stands to be significant. A 2.35x bandwidth increase on its own is quite remarkable. Accomplishing that while also shrinking the width of a DIMM by 44% is even more so. Consequently, DDR6 as currently proposed stands to be a big change indeed.

As for when we might see a complete specification, or better still physical DIMMs, that will have to wait. This preview was just that: an early look at a specification still under development, and a not-too-subtle reminder to the industry that if they want to see more and participate in the development process, they need to be part of the JEDEC. On which note, the JC-42 workgroup will be meeting in Hawaii at the end of this month for their final quarterly meeting of the year.
